questiontext.text:
Goal

Write two functions that return a solar panel's output for one day and for a week.

How this works in Python

A Java method carries a queue of keywords before you ever reach its name.

static int panelOutput(int hours, int rating) {
    return hours * rating;
}

Python writes the same idea like this.

def panel_output(hours, rating):
    return hours * rating

Read the differences one at a time.

  • def starts the definition. There is no static, no access modifier and no return type in front of the name.
  • Parameters are bare names. You never write a type in front of a parameter, and you never write one after it either.
  • The header ends with a colon and the body is indented under it, exactly as an if body is. Indentation does the work braces did in Java.
  • return value hands a value back to the caller, the same way it does in Java.
  • Calling looks the same as Java. panel_output(6, 250) runs the body and gives back its result.

Function names follow the convention variable names follow. Words go in lower case and join with underscores, so Java's panelOutput becomes panel_output.

Break one habit before you start. Printing and returning are separate acts. print puts text on the screen and hands back nothing. return hands a value to whoever called the function and puts nothing on the screen. The tests below print what your function returns, so a function that prints instead of returning shows None and fails.

Your task
  • panel_output(hours, rating) returns the output for one day, which is hours multiplied by rating.
  • weekly_output(hours, rating) returns seven days of that figure. Work it out by calling panel_output and multiplying its result by 7. Do not repeat the multiplication that panel_output already does.

Each function is one line of body. If yours is longer, you have written Java. You pass when both functions return the numbers the tests expect.

Rules
  • Return the number. Print it inside the function and the test prints None underneath, and you fail.
  • Do not write a type in front of a parameter, and do not write one after it either. hours: int fails the checker.
  • Do not put a return type on the header. Python has no -> in this topic.
  • weekly_output must call panel_output. Rewriting the multiplication yourself fails the checker.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

No AI. Type every character yourself. This tier builds the muscle, and a tool that types it for you skips the exercise.

testcode.text: print(weekly_output(1, 1)) print(panel_output(0, 250)) day_one = panel_output(2, 50) day_two = panel_output(3, 50) print(day_one + day_two)

import inspect src = inspect.getsource(panel_output) week = inspect.getsource(weekly_output) assert "return" in src, "rule broken: panel_output must return its answer" assert "print" not in src, "rule broken: return the number, do not print it" assert "print" not in week, "rule broken: return the number, do not print it" assert "hours:" not in src and "rating:" not in src, "rule broken: no type on a parameter" assert "->" not in src and "->" not in week, "rule broken: no return type on the header" assert "static" not in src and "public" not in src, "rule broken: Python has no static and no public" assert "panel_output(" in week, "rule broken: weekly_output must call panel_output" print(panel_output(4, 125)) print(weekly_output(4, 125))

questiontext.text:
Goal

Write one name at the left margin and four functions covering paired return values, the implicit None, and local scope.

How this works in Python

A Java method hands back one thing. When you need two, you invent a container for them.

static int[] summarise(int[] readings) {
    int count = 0, total = 0;
    for (int r : readings) { count++; total += r; }
    return new int[] {count, total};
}

Python returns both and skips the container.

def summarise(readings):
    ...
    return count, total

The comma is the whole trick. Python bundles the two values into a tuple, a fixed group of values that cannot be changed once made. Printing one shows round brackets and commas.

print(summarise([4, 5, 6]))     # (3, 15)

The caller can also spread the bundle across two names in one line. A later topic covers tuples in full. Two facts carry you through this exercise.

count, total = summarise([4, 5, 6])
print(count, total)             # 3 15

Next, the function that hands back nothing. Java makes you write void and then refuses to compile int x = doThing();. Python has no void. A function that reaches its end without a return hands back None, Python's null, and the caller is free to print it.

Last, where a name lives. In Java, assigning to a field inside a method changes the field. Python works the other way round. A name you assign inside a function is local to that call, and it disappears when the call ends. It never touches a name of the same spelling written at the left margin of the file.

threshold = 5

def tighten():
    threshold = 1        # a new local name, not the one above
    return threshold

print(tighten())         # 1
print(threshold)         # 5, untouched

Reading works differently from assigning. A function that only reads threshold, and never assigns to it, sees the value at the left margin.

The empty list is the case a careless answer fails. Count and total both start at zero, so the loop body never runs and the pair comes back as zeros.

Your task
  • Keep threshold at the left margin, bound to 5.
  • summarise(readings) loops over the readings and returns two numbers, how many there were and what they add up to, in that order. An empty list returns 0 and 0.
  • clear_log() prints log cleared and holds no return statement at all.
  • over_threshold(reading) returns whether reading is greater than threshold. Read the name, do not assign to it.
  • tighten() binds a local threshold to 1 and returns it. The one at the left margin must survive unchanged.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text exactly.

Rules
  • Hand back both numbers from summarise with a single return and a comma. No list, no wrapper.
  • Do not call len or sum. Count and add inside the loop.
  • Leave clear_log with no return statement.
  • Do not write global or nonlocal anywhere. Reaching out of a function to rebind a name is the habit this exercise is breaking.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

AI for explanation only. Ask it what an error means or why one form is more idiomatic. Do not let it write your answer.

testcode.text: print(summarise([4, 5, 6])) count, total = summarise([2, 2]) print(count, total) print(summarise([]))

import inspect sm = inspect.getsource(summarise) cl = inspect.getsource(clear_log) tg = inspect.getsource(tighten) ot = inspect.getsource(over_threshold) assert "len(" not in sm and "sum(" not in sm, "rule broken: count and add inside the loop" assert "return" in sm, "rule broken: summarise must hand back both numbers" assert "return" not in cl, "rule broken: clear_log must have no return statement" for source in (sm, cl, tg, ot): assert "global" not in source, "rule broken: do not write global" assert "nonlocal" not in source, "rule broken: do not write nonlocal" print(summarise([10])) print(summarise([1, 2, 3, 4])) n, amount = summarise([7, 8]) print(n) print(amount) print(tighten()) print(threshold)

questiontext.text:
Goal

Write a collatz_steps function that returns a step count and a log_start function that returns nothing.

How this works in Python

A Java method needs a return type, and often several keywords, in front of its name.

static int collatzSteps(int n) {
    int steps = 0;
    while (n != 1) {
        n = (n % 2 == 0) ? n / 2 : 3 * n + 1;
        steps++;
    }
    return steps;
}

Python drops all of that.

def collatz_steps(n):
    steps = 0
    while n != 1:
        ...
        steps = steps + 1
    return steps
  • def starts a function. There is no return type, no static, no access modifier and no throws clause.
  • The header ends with a colon and the body is indented, exactly as an if body is.
  • return value hands a value back to the caller, the same way it does in Java.
  • A function that reaches its end without a return hands back None. None is Python's null. Java refuses to compile a method that misses a return. Python runs that function and says nothing.
  • while condition: repeats the body for as long as the condition holds. It works as Java's while does, without the parentheses and with a colon on the end.
  • There is no ++ and no --. Write steps = steps + 1 instead. The text ++steps reads as two plus signs in front of a number and changes nothing at all.

Two arithmetic operators appear in this exercise. n % 2 is the remainder, as in Java. n // 2 divides and throws the remainder away, which is what / does on two Java ints. A single / in Python always gives a float, so 6 / 2 is 3.0.

The loops topic gave you the indented loop body. The indentation topic gave you the branch that catches an n of 1 or less.

Your task
  • collatz_steps(n) counts the steps needed to reach 1. Halve n with // when it is even. Replace n with 3 * n + 1 when it is odd. Count every replacement, then return the count once n reaches 1. Return 0 for any n of 1 or less, before the loop starts.
  • log_start() prints logger armed and holds no return statement at all. A hidden test prints its result, so you see None appear underneath.

You pass when collatz_steps(6) returns 8 and collatz_steps(7) returns 16. The tests print those return values, so a function that prints instead of returning shows None and fails.

Rules
  • Return the count. Print it inside the function and the test prints None underneath, and you fail.
  • Use while for the loop. for is banned in this one exercise.
  • Do not write ++ or --. Python has neither.
  • Call no builtin except print. No sum, no max, no min, no abs, no len.
  • Leave log_start with no return statement.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

AI allowed, on three conditions. Write your plan before you open it. Read every suggestion and reject the ones you did not plan. Type accepted code out yourself rather than pressing Tab.

testcode.text: import inspect src = inspect.getsource(collatz_steps) assert "while" in src, "rule broken: the loop must be a while" assert "for " not in src, "rule broken: no for loop in this one" assert "return" in src, "rule broken: the function must return its answer" assert "print" not in src, "rule broken: return the count, do not print it" assert "++" not in src and "--" not in src, "rule broken: Python has no ++ or --" for name in ("sum(", "max(", "min(", "abs(", "len("): assert name not in src, "rule broken: no builtin except print" assert "return" not in inspect.getsource(log_start), "rule broken: log_start must not return" print(collatz_steps(12)) print(log_start())
